concept: Shipped frontend code is public
points: Everything the browser downloads, including JavaScript bundles and any keys or URLs inside them, can be read by anyone. Wiz found Moltbook's Supabase project URL and key in a production Next.js chunk that loads automatically with the page.
Attackers do not use your UI. They take what is in the bundle and call your backend API directly. Wiz sent its own query to Supabase's REST API with the key from the bundle.
Code that runs in the browser cannot keep a secret. Calls that need a secret belong in server code: Lovable moves API calls server-side, and v0 refactors them into Route Handlers or Server Actions.
gap: Builders picture the UI as the boundary ('people can only do what my buttons allow'). Moltbook's founder said he wrote none of the code himself. Researchers browsing as ordinary visitors read the bundle and queried the database directly (S044). Lovable's docs state that frontend code cannot safely hold secrets (S045).
humanRole: The agent can move secret calls server-side and search the built bundle for keys when asked. The human must know the browser is not a boundary. They must ask for the deployed app to be tested as an outsider would test it (read the shipped bundle, call the API without the UI), and decide which values are allowed to be public at all.
outdated: Users can only do what the buttons let them do
A minified bundle hides what is inside it
questions: Can people see my code once my site is deployed?
If there is no button for it, can someone still do it?
Where should my API calls live?
demo: Open a deployed test app, go to DevTools > Sources (or Network), and search the loaded JavaScript for the backend URL or a key name. Then send the same request from a terminal with curl, skipping the UI entirely.

concept: Supabase publishable (anon) key is public by design; RLS is the lock
points: The Supabase publishable key is meant to sit in the browser and works like a project identifier. Whether data is safe depends entirely on row-level security (RLS) policies.

Without RLS policies, that key gives full database access to anyone who has it. At Moltbook this exposed 1.5 million agent API tokens, about 35,000 email addresses, and 4,060 private DM conversations, some containing OpenAI keys.
A correctly protected table answers an anonymous request with an empty array or an authorization error. If rows come back, the table is open.
With RLS enabled and no policies written, the publishable key gets no data at all through the API.
Wiz traced the root cause to one configuration setting, not to the visible key.
gap: Beginners either panic that the key is visible or assume a key labeled 'anon' must be harmless. Wiz says today's AI tools do not yet reason about access control on the developer's behalf. Moltbook was vibe-coded end to end and shipped with no RLS (S044).
humanRole: The agent can write RLS policies and run the anonymous-key test itself. The human must require that test against the live project for every table, rather than accepting the statement 'RLS is enabled', and must know how to read the result: rows returned means the table is open.
outdated: A visible key means I have been hacked
The anon key is harmless because it is anonymous
questions: Is it safe that my Supabase key is in my frontend code?
What is RLS and do I need it?
How do I know whether my database is open to the world?
demo: In a throwaway Supabase project, create a table without RLS. Use curl to query /rest/v1/<table>?select=* with the publishable key in the apikey header and watch rows come back. Enable RLS with no policy, run the same request again, and get an empty array.

concept: Grants, policies and default exposure of new Supabase tables
points: Grants and policies are separate checks. A grant decides whether a role may run an operation on a table at all. An RLS policy decides which rows that operation can touch.

On existing Supabase projects, a new table in the public schema starts with select, insert, update and delete granted to anon, authenticated and service_role. Some projects do not grant these automatically.
Supabase says it is changing the platform default so that exposure becomes opt-in. The docs give no date for this change.

Adding policies does not take grants back. A table protected only by policies can still hand anon an insert path if the grant is never revoked. The docs advise granting each role only the operations it needs.
An event trigger can enable RLS automatically on every new table. If the app does not use the Data API, it can be switched off entirely, and then none of the auto-generated endpoints respond.
gap: 'RLS enabled' is treated as a single on/off safe state. The Supabase docs show two layers (grants, then policies) and default grants on new tables. Because RLS is set per table, every new table an agent creates is a new exposure (S044, Supabase RLS and Securing-your-API docs).
humanRole: The agent can write the SQL that revokes default privileges and the event trigger that enables RLS on new tables. The human must find out which default their project uses, and must require the outsider test to be rerun after every schema change, because a safe state on one table does not carry over to the next one.
outdated: RLS on means secure
Supabase tables are private until I share them
New tables inherit the protection of old ones
questions: I enabled RLS, so why can anonymous users still insert rows?
Do new tables get my security settings automatically?
demo: Create a new table in a test Supabase project, inspect which privileges anon holds on it, then attempt an insert with the publishable key from curl.

concept: Secret / service_role key bypasses RLS and must never reach the browser
points: Supabase secret keys, and the legacy JWT service_role key, act as the service_role Postgres role, which has the bypassrls attribute.
The docs say never to use a secret key in the browser or expose it to customers. It belongs only in server code, for admin tasks.
A secret key bypasses RLS only when the request carries no user access token. With a user token attached, the request runs under that user's policies.
In Next.js, only variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ reach the browser, so a service key stored under a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name ships to every visitor.
gap: The two key types look alike. When RLS blocks a query, the quickest 'fix' is to swap in the key that works, and that turns all protection off. Sources: Supabase RLS docs (read for S044) and v0's NEXT_PUBLIC_ rule (S045).
humanRole: The agent can search client code and the built bundle for the secret key. The human must know that two classes of key exist, refuse any fix that makes an error go away by moving the secret key to the client, and keep the secret key only in server-side environment variables.
outdated: If the query fails, use the other key
All Supabase keys are equivalent
questions: What is the difference between the publishable (anon) key and the secret (service_role) key?
My query works with the service key but not the anon key. Which should I use?
demo: Build a test Next.js app with a dummy value stored under a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name. Open the page and find that value in the JavaScript the browser loaded.

concept: Views and security-definer functions bypass RLS
points: Postgres creates views as security definer, owned by the postgres user, so they bypass RLS by default. A view over a protected table can hand out every row its policies were meant to withhold.
The fix on Postgres 15 and later is security_invoker = true. On older versions, revoke access from anon and authenticated, or move the view to a schema the API does not expose.
A security-definer function in an exposed schema can be called over the Data API with its creator's privileges.
gap: A table can pass an RLS check while a view or function built on it leaks the same rows. The Supabase RLS docs (read for S044) warn about exactly this.
humanRole: The agent can audit views and functions and set security_invoker. The human must ask for the audit to cover views and functions, not only tables, and make sure the anonymous test also queries the views.
outdated: If the table has RLS, everything built on it is protected
questions: My table has RLS. Can a view still leak its data?
demo: In a test project, create a view over an RLS-protected table and query the view with the publishable key: rows come back. Set security_invoker = true and query it again.

concept: Read protection is not write protection; fixes come in rounds
points: Moltbook's first fixes stopped reads, but the public tables could still be written to. Wiz edited a live post as a test.
Write access allows defacement and the planting of prompt-injection payloads, which other AI agents then read.
The fixes came in six rounds over about three hours. Each round turned up more open tables, including observers, identity_verifications and developer_apps.
gap: People test 'can strangers see my data?' and stop there. Even after a responsible disclosure, Moltbook's first fix left writes open (S044).
humanRole: The agent can write insert, update and delete policies and test them. The human must require tests for all four operations (read, insert, update, delete), run both as a stranger and as a different logged-in user, and rerun them after every round of fixes.
outdated: Data that is public anyway does not need protecting
One fix closes the hole
questions: My data is public anyway, so why does write access matter?
We fixed the reported issue. Are we done?
demo: Using only the publishable key, send a POST or PATCH from curl to a table in a test project and see whether the change goes through.

concept: NEXT_PUBLIC_ and similar prefixes publish a value to every visitor
points: In Next.js, only environment variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are exposed to the browser. Variables without the prefix stay on the server.
v0 tells you never to expose sensitive tokens with the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix. It analyzes NEXT_PUBLIC_ usage and warns about risks.
If a key must stay secret, the fix is to move the call into a Route Handler or Server Action, not to rename the variable.
gap: When a key 'does not work' in client code, adding the prefix makes the error disappear, and quietly publishes the key. v0 builds warnings for this because it is a common mistake (S045).
humanRole: The agent can refactor calls to the server side. The human must treat the prefix as a publishing decision and check that every NEXT_PUBLIC_ value is something they would post on a public page.
outdated: Environment variables are always secret
questions: Why is my environment variable undefined in the browser?
Is it safe to put my OpenAI key in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable?
demo: Add a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable with a dummy value to a test Next.js app, build it, open the page, and search the loaded JavaScript for the value.

concept: Environments: separate Development, Preview and Production keys
points: On v0 and Vercel, each environment variable is assigned to Production (the live app), Preview (deployments from non-production branches) and/or Development (the v0 preview panel or local runs).
The v0 preview can only see Development variables. Naming trap: v0's 'preview' panel is the Development environment, not Vercel's Preview environment.
v0's best practice is to use different keys for development and production, and to rotate keys and secrets regularly.
Variables are stored encrypted on Vercel and set under Project > Settings > Environment Variables, not written into code.
gap: Beginners use one key everywhere, and get confused when something works in the preview but not in production. The per-environment rules are on v0's External APIs page, not its Security page (S045).
humanRole: The human owns the provider accounts that issue keys. They must create separate development and production keys, set each in the right environment, and rotate them on a schedule and after any suspected leak. The agent can wire the code to read the variables.
outdated: One API key for everything
If it works in the preview it works live
questions: Why does my app work in the v0 preview but not after I publish?
Do I need different keys for testing and production?
demo: Open a v0 project's Settings > Environment Variables and show the environment choices attached to a variable.

concept: Builder security scans are a floor, not a certification
points: Lovable's Quick scan runs when you open the publish dialog. It checks database access rules, npm dependency vulnerabilities, and MCP servers exposed without authentication.

The Deep scan covers access control, unauthenticated endpoints, injection, leaked secrets, payments, authentication and sensitive-data exposure. It does not run automatically during development; you have to start it.
Auto-fix handles only Quick-scan findings. Only critical dependency vulnerabilities are surfaced, and some are suppressed by EPSS score.

Lovable says its tools cannot guarantee complete security and do not replace a thorough security review, and that the user is responsible. It recommends a professional review for apps with sensitive data. Its Trust center page is informational, not a certification.

Lovable advises reviewing RLS before publishing and after changes to authentication or database structure. Scan results show 'Up to date' only for the current version, so scans must be rerun after changes.
v0's own threat model treats all generated code as potentially incorrect or adversarial.
gap: A green scan, or the agent saying 'your app is secure', is taken as a verdict. The platforms themselves say it is not one (S045). Wiz notes that AI tools do not yet reason about security posture for you (S044).
humanRole: The agent can run scans and fix what they find. The human must run the Deep scan (not only the Quick scan), rerun it after schema or auth changes, read the findings instead of clicking 'fix all', and for apps holding personal, payment or other sensitive data, bring in a professional reviewer.
outdated: The security scan passed, so the app is safe
The AI said it is secure
questions: Lovable says my app passed the security scan. Am I safe?
When do I need a real security review?
demo: Open Lovable's Security view and show the Quick and Deep scan buttons and the 'Up to date' indicator. Make a schema change and watch the indicator go stale.

concept: Public means found within days: newly registered sites are scanned
points: METR suspects an attacker found a researcher's app by scanning recently registered websites, for example in certificate-transparency lists. The attacker was looking for vibe-coded sites with LLM or agent keywords, to harvest model-provider keys.
The app was exposed for several days and was found within that window. A new public URL has no period of obscurity.
The May 2026 campaign against METR was heavily automated: credential stuffing, OAuth token-grant attempts, scanning of newly deployed services, and phishing of staff.
gap: Side-project builders assume nobody knows the URL. METR's post shows attackers systematically sweeping new sites for AI keys (S046).
humanRole: Assume the site will be discovered as soon as it is deployed. Before anything goes public, the human decides what it may hold (no production keys, no private data) and checks access from outside. The agent cannot know whether a deploy was meant to be public.
outdated: Nobody will find my side project
An unlisted URL is private
questions: Who would ever find my little app?
Is an unlisted URL private?
demo: Deploy a test site to a fresh subdomain, then search a public certificate-transparency log for that domain and show the new certificate already listed.

concept: Auth that fails open
points: METR's vibe-coded app sat behind Google authentication, but a fail-open vulnerability silently disabled the login. The app kept working, so nothing looked wrong.
It stayed exposed for several days. The attacker took the API key and added an SSH key so the access would persist.
METR now requires a security review for any researcher who deploys an app publicly.
gap: A login screen does not mean the app is protected, and owners usually test while logged in (S046).
humanRole: The agent can write tests that call protected routes without a session. The human must demand those tests, check the app from a logged-out browser or another device after each deploy, and insist that auth fails closed (denies access when anything errors).
outdated: It has a login, so it is private
questions: How do I check that my login actually protects my pages?
What does 'fail open' mean?
demo: Open the deployed app in a private window, then request a protected page or API route with curl and no cookie. Check whether it returns data or a 401 / redirect.

concept: An agent holding a key can be asked to reveal it
points: The METR attacker simply prompted the exposed agent to reveal its model-provider API key.
On Moltbook, agents' private DMs held plaintext OpenAI keys that agents had shared with each other.
In n8n, anyone with API access can build a workflow that uses a stored OpenAI credential without ever seeing it, or one that sends the raw credential to an external listener.
Anyone who can talk to an agent or automation, or control it, can try to extract whatever it can read or use.
gap: People treat the agent as a safe container for credentials. Three incidents show keys pulled out through the agent or automation itself (S046, S044, S048).
humanRole: The human decides which keys an agent gets: scoped, spend-limited, revocable keys only. A publicly reachable agent should never hold a key the human could not afford to lose. The agent cannot guarantee it will not disclose what it holds.
outdated: The key is safe because only the agent can see it
questions: Can someone get my API key out of my chatbot?
Is it safe to give my agent my OpenAI key?
demo: Run a local test agent with a dummy key in its environment, ask it to show its configuration or environment, and show it repeating the dummy key.

concept: Spend limits and usage alerts on every API key
points: A stolen METR key was used for about three weeks to consume credits worth about $600,000.

Nobody noticed for three reasons: rate-limit errors were routine during evaluations, the dashboard did not show rate-limited requests for all users, and the credits were free, so no bill spiked. That key type could not take a spending limit.
Afterwards, METR added spend alerts where possible, and monitoring for unusual key usage.
Budget alerts alone do not stop spending. A hard cap needs a 'stop usage when the budget is reached' setting, as GitHub notes for AI Credits.
gap: Beginners never set caps, and free credits feel risk-free. The METR loss went unseen for weeks (S046). GitHub warns that budget alerts are not limits (S047, 2026-10-07 changelog).
humanRole: Only the account owner can set spend caps and alerts in the provider's dashboard. The human must set hard limits (not just alerts) on every key and actually look at usage instead of dismissing errors as noise. The agent has no access to billing settings.
outdated: Free credits mean no risk
A budget alert will stop the spending
questions: How do I stop a leaked key from running up a huge bill?
Is a budget alert the same as a limit?
demo: Open an AI provider's billing or limits page and show the difference between an alert threshold and a hard cap.

concept: Keep public apps away from private data
points: METR's public transcript viewer exposed a read-only SQL query feature. It was scoped to public data by default, but a bug could reach unpublished data, and the database also held some more-sensitive data by accident.
METR brought the endpoint back after a few days without noticing the bug. An independent researcher found it, and METR paid a bounty.

METR then built a public production environment that is architecturally separate from internal infrastructure, so a misconfigured public service cannot expose internal data. It also shortened credential lifetimes and reduced permission scopes.
Moltbook kept agent tokens, owner emails, private DMs and signup lists in one database, so one setting exposed all of them.
gap: 'Read-only' and 'scoped to public data' feel safe, but one bug crosses the line whenever private data shares the same store (S046, S044).
humanRole: The human decides what data the public-facing app can reach at all (a separate database, project or keys for public and private data). The agent cannot infer which data is private. The agent can then build that separation.
outdated: Read-only access cannot leak anything
questions: Can my public site and my private data share a database?
demo: No on-screen demo. A diagram of the public app's reach (what its keys can touch) before and after the separation would show it.

concept: Automation-platform tokens have a huge blast radius
points: An n8n API token can reach users, workflows (including secrets hard-coded in them), credential metadata, full execution payloads, data tables, variables, and an audit report that maps the instance's weaknesses.
With that access, an attacker can create workflows that use stored credentials or send them out. Deleting the workflow also deletes its execution records.
GitGuardian demonstrated all of this using only documented API calls, without exploiting any vulnerability.
The leaked commit usually contained the instance URL next to the token, and many of the tokens belonged to owners or admins.
Public commits held 4,576 unique tokens, and 321 live instances accepted a leaked one.
gap: An automation token is thought of as one key, but it unlocks every credential the platform stores for source control, databases, cloud, AI APIs and customer data (S048).
humanRole: The human must treat automation platforms as high-risk: least-privilege API keys with expiry set, and secrets kept in the credential store rather than in workflow nodes. After a leak: revoke, audit, and rotate every connected credential. The agent can help list everything the token could reach.
outdated: It is just my n8n key
questions: What can someone do with my n8n API key?
If my automation token leaked, do I need to rotate my other keys?
demo: In a local test n8n instance, call GET /api/v1/workflows with the X-N8N-API-KEY header and show the full workflow definitions that come back.

concept: Coding-agent permission files and MCP configs leak secrets
points: When you approve an agent's curl command that contains a key, the whole command (instance URL and X-N8N-API-KEY header included) can be saved as an allow rule in .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json.
These files can be committed without the .gitignore protection that .env files usually get.

GitGuardian found 24,008 unique secrets in MCP-related config files on public GitHub in 2025, and 2,117 of them (8.8%) were verified as working. The top valid types include Google API keys and PostgreSQL connection strings.
Official MCP quickstarts often show keys written inline in the config JSON or as CLI arguments, or full postgresql://user:password@ connection strings.

GitGuardian's advice: no secrets in MCP configs (use environment variables managed by a secrets manager), MCP config folders in .gitignore, scan before pushing, and human approval for MCP actions that touch production.
gap: People .gitignore their .env but not the config files their agent tools create, so the URL and key leak together (S048, plus GitGuardian's State of Secrets Sprawl 2026).
humanRole: The human must know which files their agent tools write, check them before making a repo public, and keep keys out of the commands they approve (reference environment variables instead). When told to, the agent can add these files to .gitignore and run a secret scanner before pushing.
outdated: .env is the only file with secrets
Config files are not code, so they are safe to commit
questions: Which files in my project can contain secrets?
Is it safe to commit my .claude folder or my MCP config?
demo: In a test project, approve a curl command that carries a dummy key, then open .claude/settings.local.json to show the key saved in the allow list, and run git status to show the file is ready to be committed.

concept: Leaked secrets stay valid: revoke and rotate, do not just delete
points: Of the valid secrets GitGuardian found in 2022, 64% were still valid when retested in January 2026.
Teams avoid rotating keys because the keys are copied into many places and rotation can break production.

Older n8n keys have no expiry. A 30-day default arrived in n8n 1.78.0 (February 2025), but many tokens were created without one. Revoking the key in n8n's database kills it even though its signature is still valid.
Git history keeps old versions. In one real case, an SSH deploy key in an earlier backup commit was still valid.
The steps after a leak: revoke the key, work out what it could reach, look for unauthorized changes, and rotate every connected credential.
Disclosure rarely leads to a fix: four of the seven organizations GitGuardian contacted never responded.
gap: People delete the file or the commit and consider the leak handled (S048, plus GitGuardian's State of Secrets Sprawl 2026).
humanRole: Revoking and rotating happen in provider dashboards that the human controls. The human must do it immediately, set an expiry on new keys, and check the provider's logs for use of the leaked key. The agent can find every place the key is used and update configuration after rotation.
outdated: I deleted the commit, so the key is safe
Making the repo private fixes it
questions: I pushed my API key to GitHub. What do I do?
Is deleting the commit enough?
demo: In a test repository, commit a dummy key, delete it in a later commit, then run git log -p to show the key still sitting in history.

concept: What GitHub secret scanning and push protection actually cover
points: Push protection for users is on by default, on GitHub.com only. It blocks you from pushing supported secret types to public repositories, and a bypass creates no alert unless repository protection is also on.
Repository push protection is off by default. It needs GitHub Secret Protection, and an admin, organization owner or security manager has to enable it.
Anyone with write access can bypass a block by giving a reason ('used in tests', 'false positive' or 'I'll fix it later'). Organizations can restrict who is allowed to bypass.
Partner secrets found in public repositories are reported to the issuer automatically so they can be revoked. User secrets only raise alerts.
Detectors added on 2026-10-05: lovable_api_key (a partner secret), logfire_token, pydantic_ai_gateway_api_key, supabase_oauth_access_token and supabase_scoped_personal_access_token.

Keys from new vendors slip past until detectors catch up: GitGuardian counted 113,000 new DeepSeek keys leaked in 2025, and says push protection holds down the density of leaks but cannot stop the growing volume.
gap: Beginners believe GitHub will stop them from pushing a secret, but coverage is limited by key format, by repository visibility, and by settings that are off by default (S047, S048).
humanRole: The human must turn on repository push protection where it is available, never click bypass for a real key, and not rely on GitHub for secrets without a known format or from new vendors. The agent can run a local secret scanner before each push.
outdated: GitHub will not let me push a secret
A private repo is safe to hold keys
questions: Does GitHub block secrets automatically?
What happens if I bypass push protection?
demo: Push a commit containing a dummy token in a supported format to a public test repository and show the push-protection block and its bypass options.

concept: Model-based secret detection (October 2026): new, mostly opt-in, billed
points: GitHub's fine-tuned model looks at the code around a match to judge whether it is really a credential, and can flag passwords that have no recognizable token format.
Existing AI-detected password alerts moved to the new model automatically, and are included with GitHub Secret Protection or Advanced Security.
AI push protection is in private preview. It is off by default, an admin must opt in, and it is billed as AI Credits even when it does not block a push.
Secret checks in Copilot's /security-review command are announced for an upcoming private preview and will be off by default.
Budget alerts do not stop AI Credit spending. A cap requires the 'Stop usage when budget limit is reached' setting.
gap: Pattern detection cannot see plain passwords or other unformatted secrets. The capability that can is new and is not switched on by default (S047 companion: GitHub Changelog, 2026-10-07).
humanRole: An organization admin decides whether to opt in and caps the spend. Nobody should assume this coverage exists unless they have checked that it is turned on.
outdated: Secret scanning only finds keys with known prefixes (now partly untrue, but only where enabled)
questions: Will GitHub catch a plain password in my code?

concept: AI co-authored commits: leak rate and larger diffs
points: In 2025, 1.5% of 1.94 billion public commits contained an exposed credential. Commits co-authored by Claude Code contained one 3.2% of the time.

The Claude Code rate peaked at 31 secrets per 1,000 commits in August 2025, about 2.4x the human baseline. By December it was 13 per 1,000, matching the baseline. GitGuardian links the drop to the release of Claude Sonnet 4.5 in late September 2025.
From April 2025, Claude Code commits averaged about twice as many lines as human commits. The gap evened out by year end.
GitGuardian says the developer remains in control of the commit. It recommends treating large AI change sets as higher-impact review units and keeping automated scanning in the workflow.
Commits were classified as AI co-authored by a Co-Authored-By trailer carrying a known AI tool email.
gap: Beginners assume the agent will never commit a secret. The opposite outdated view, that AI commits leak twice as much, is a 2025 annual average that had converged with the human rate by December (S048, plus GitGuardian's State of Secrets Sprawl 2026).
humanRole: The commit belongs to the human. They must make sure a secret scan runs before every push, and review large AI-written changes as high-impact. The agent can run the scanner and keep keys in environment variables, but the human decides what gets pushed.
outdated: AI commits leak secrets twice as often (stated as a current fact)
The agent will not commit my keys
questions: Does using Claude Code make me more likely to leak keys?
demo: Run git log on a project built with an agent to show Co-Authored-By trailers, then run a secret scanner over the history.
